newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Bank of England ups interest rate to 6.75%.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Bank of England ups interest rate to 6.75%.

text.p: The Bank of England raised official interest rates to 6.75 percent from 6.50 percent on Thursday in an attempt to cool consumer demand and meet the government's inflation target.
The quarter point rise, the third in as many months, was widely anticipated by financial markets, but that did not prevent a volatile reaction from the pound.

It see-sawed against the German mark, dropping over one pfennig, bouncing smartly, then falling again. Foreign exchange traders said they were disappointed the rate rise was a only a quarter and not a half point.

The central bank said the pound's 11-month rally, which has punished British manufacturers who need to sell their goods abroad, complicated the rate decision but the recent run of economic data showing strong consumer spending had, in the end, forced its hand.

"The upward revision of estimated output growth in the fourth quarter of 1996 and recent development in monetary growth and retail sales indicated that a further tightening of monetary policy was necessary," the Bank said in a statement.
The government immediately backed the rate rise and Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown said the former Conservative administration failed to control inflation.

"Today the Bank of England has agreed with me that we must prevent a return to the boom-and-bust and that inflationary pressures in the economy which, despite persistent warning the previous government negligently failed to tackle, must be brought under control," he said in a statement.

However, most of Britain's millions of home-owners will, for the moment, escape the impact of the Bank's move. Of the big lenders, only Abbey Plc passed on the rate rise, pushing up its variable rate by 25 basis points.
The Halifax, Britain's biggest mortgage lender, Nationwide, Britain's largest building society, and the Woolwich all said they would take no immediate action but were reviewing situation.
But home owners lucky enough to get away with unchanged mortgage rates this time are unlikely to avoid higher charges for long.
Most City economists agreed there are more interest rate rises in the pipeline, maybe as soon as next month.
"This quarter point rise is whistling in the wind as far as slowing down consumer growth is concerned," said Michael Dicks, UK economist at Lehman Brothers.
He forecasts a series of quarter point rises, with interest rates peaking at 8.0 percent next summer.
He said the timing of the next move depends on whether the strong consumer spending seen in May continues during the summer.
"If retail sales slow down a bit and price pressures are seen easing the Bank might be prepared to wait until September before moving again."
Data covering the summer months will provide crucial information about the impact big windfall payments from building society flotations are having on the economy.

The Bank of England has said it is very concerned the windfall cash, set to total 35 billion pounds this year alone, will turn robust consumer spending into a runaway boom and lead to higher prices on the high street.
Inflation is currently above the government's target. Underlying retail prices edged up to 2.7 percent in the year to June, overshooting the 2.5 percent goal.
Financial markets have factored in another quarter point rate rise by the end of September and another by December.
The pound steadied around the day's lows and stood at 2.9541/50 marks in late afternoon trade, down two pfennigs from Wednesday.

Government bonds gained modestly on the rate rise but slipped lower by the end of the session. The September gilt future traded on the LIFFE exchange stood at 114-06 in late trade, down 3/32 on the day.
Shares pared early losses after the rate rise and ended the day in positive territory. The FTSE index of 100 leading shares stood at 4766.7, up 4.3 on the day.
